topComments.author: bombcar
topComments.text: What I did on our WordPress boxes while waiting for distro packages (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) 1. session.upload_progress.enabled = Off, in php.ini and as php_admin_flag in every FPM pool, so per-directory config can't turn it back on. It's one of the two confirmed consumers in GHSA-6wmf, and the validated FPM path depends on it. Almost nobody uses it, and the advisory suggests leaving it off even after patching. 2. Refuse multipart request bodies at the web server, before PHP parses them. All of the GHSA-w8hw out-of-memory strategies go through multipart parsing. On Apache it's a rewrite rule matching a Content-Type of multipart/form-data that returns 403. On Caddy it's a header matcher that responds 403. The cost: every browser upload breaks (media library, plugin zips, importers). Check your public forms first. 3. Check your SAPI. Both bugs have confirmed RCE against mod_php. FPM is narrower: the validated path needs upload_progress, and the early INI consumer only applies if your front end sends PHP_VALUE/PHP_ADMIN_VALUE. To check, grep your Apache, nginx and Caddy configs for it, and run apache2ctl -M | grep php. 4. pm.max_requests = 1 in the pools. A worker serves one request and exits, which breaks the stale-state chain: the "producer" and "consumer" requests must land on the same worker. It costs a fork per request. 5. Lower max_input_nesting_level and post_max_size, per the advisory. 6. Housekeeping that should already be done: no .php served from uploads directories, and remove any stray phpinfo.php. Scanners request it constantly, and it tells an attacker your exact build.

stories.title: The Decoherence Trap
stories.author: cassianoleal

topComments.author: torben-friis
topComments.text: Apologies for opening the discussion with a half related topic, since I haven't finished the article yet, but... Damn, that is one beautiful website. Edit: Back after reading. I think I have a point about the simulation section. It compares the difference in decoherence introduced in the system by clankers and human devs as if those were different groups. I suspect if we consider AI a human performance multiplier, we explain easily how supercharging a dysfunctional process just makes it go sideways faster. There are organizational experiments to try there. For example, what if you only supercharge a section of the company tasked with maintaining coherence? A common organizational problem is that the people who know and care about the system itself are outnumbered by the rest (juniors, people new to the system, managers rushing jobs, people who want to mark things as done ASAP tactically, etc). This imbalance will multiply when code is mass produced and reviews are dismissed. We're all seeing the senior burnout and cynical YOLOing occurring everywhere. AI offers a way to rebalance this dynamic, though. You can effectively add multipliers to arbitrary human workers, and get a system that tends to low complexity by design. You don't have to renounce to speed either. The junior dev will be faster not by being AI-enabled, but by working in an adaptable, understandable system.

topComments.author: souvik1997
topComments.text: Looks cool! One aspect of multi-user agent security, which I think is underexplored, is how context from a higher-privileged session might "leak" into a lower privileged session. Suppose the CEO of a company uses your shared openclaw agent and the agent writes sensitive data (investor emails, for example) to its memory. My understanding is this is not protected by Alter. Then a contractor uses the same agent and can read that same memory. It seems to me that a better agent harness for this kind of multi-user use case is needed; the standard ones like openclaw and claude code simply are not designed for it. Would love your thoughts!

topComments.author: avikonduru
topComments.text: How do you handle permissions when the downstream service only offers a shared API key? For example, two sales reps can use the same CRM endpoint but should only access their own accounts. Does Alter check record ownership, or does the developer still need to supply that logic?

topComments.author: 911viper
topComments.text: Following the same thread as souvik1997 here: the leak problem gets worse in shared rooms than in shared sessions. When several principals (humans plus their own agents) sit in one channel, the transcript becomes the privilege boundary. Whatever an agent read in a higher-privileged turn is sitting in the context of every later turn in that room. What we hit building exactly that, rooms where humans and bots are peers: you can't scope a token to an agent, you have to scope it to an (agent, room) pair, and then decide what happens to the derived artifacts. Tool output, file handles, and the memory blob the agent writes back all outlive the session and get replayed into the next one. So how are you handling derived state? Is agent memory a new principal holding the intersection of the rights of the sessions that fed it, or does it just inherit and you rely on the model not to act on stale context?

infoqArticles.title: Netflix Bridges AWS IAM and Internal Identity with Workload Attestation
infoqArticles.description: Netflix has developed a workload attestation mechanism for Apache Spark jobs running on Amazon EMR. The design combines AWS IAM identity with signed claims from Netflix’s control plane before issuing short-lived internal X.509 certificates, allowing managed compute workloads to authenticate to internal services without directly injecting credentials. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Article Series: Agentic AI Architecture
infoqArticles.description: In this article series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. By Rafał G
infoqArticles.author: Rafał Gancarz

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: AI is an Amplifier: Scale High Performance, Not Dysfunction
infoqArticles.description: Nathen Harvey shares insights from DORA research on AI adoption in software delivery. He explains why AI acts as an amplifier, how the DORA AI Capabilities Model drives outcomes, and why engineering leaders must evolve beyond bottlenecks like code reviews to achieve sustainable productivity, reduce delivery instability, and empower developers without burning out their teams. By Nathen Harvey
infoqArticles.author: Nathen Harvey

infoqArticles.title: Google SynthID Detector Simplifies Watermark Detection and Expands Support to Other AI Providers
infoqArticles.description: Google DeepMind announced the global availability of SynthID Detector, a tool designed to help identify AI-generated content, including media created using AI tools from SynthID partners such as OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Kakao, with Apple support expected soon. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Article: Distributed Spring Batch Without a Message Broker
infoqArticles.description: Distributed Spring Batch partitioning already needs a shared, persistent job repository. This article makes that database the whole coordination plane and drops the message broker, sizing work to the live node count, a per-job master with no standing coordinator, compare-and-set claiming that prevents double-execution, two-phase heartbeat failover, and where a broker is still the right choice. By
infoqArticles.author: Janardhan Reddy Chejarla

infoqArticles.title: Cilium 1.20 Expands Gateway API and Opens eBPF Datapath for Kubernetes
infoqArticles.description: Cilium 1.20 has been released with broader Kubernetes Gateway API support, an extensible eBPF datapath and further work on sidecarless mutual TLS. The release also makes the newer netkit network device easier to introduce across Kubernetes fleets that run different Linux kernel versions. By Matt Saunders
infoqArticles.author: Matt Saunders

infoqArticles.title: Microsoft Previews dotnetup: Toolchain Manager for .NET SDKs and Runtimes
infoqArticles.description: Microsoft has released a public preview of dotnetup, a cross-platform toolchain manager that installs and updates .NET SDKs and runtimes in the user’s own directory without admin rights. It tracks channels such as latest, lts, preview, and daily, reads global.json, and removes unused installs. Commands may still change before general availability. By Almir Vuk
infoqArticles.author: Almir Vuk

infoqArticles.title: TornadoVM 7 Enables GPU-Native Workloads From Java Applications
infoqArticles.description: TornadoVM, an open-source heterogeneous programming framework for Java has reached version 7.0. It automatically accelerates Java programs on multi-core CPUs and GPUs and provides a rich GPU programming ecosystem in Java that can be used with any mainstream JDK distribution e.g. Temurin, Red Hat OpenJDK, Coretto, Oracle, GraalVM or Zulu. By Ben Evans
infoqArticles.author: Ben Evans

infoqArticles.title: GitHub Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 Targets Reliability at Scale

infoqArticles.author: Craig Risi

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Beyond the Prototype: Scaling Framework Agnostic AI Agent Infrastructure with Ray
infoqArticles.description: The speakers discuss transitioning AI agents from local FastAPI prototypes to resilient production systems on Kubernetes using Ray. They share operational insights on RayCluster topology, stateful memory handling, auto-scaling on dynamic traffic, and robust control plane designs, while highlighting critical guardrails, multi-region setups, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines. By Deepak Mohanak
infoqArticles.author: Deepak Mohanakumar Chandramouli, Bhumik Vinodkumar Thakkar

infoqArticles.title: Java News Roundup: JEPs for JDK 28, Azul Payara, Gatherers4j, Google ADK, Yupiik, Apache Camel CVEs
infoqArticles.description: This week's Java roundup for October 12th, 2026, features news highlighting: three OpenJDK JEPs targeted for JDK 28; the October 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Gatherers4j, Yupiik Fusion, Google ADK for Java and Google ADK for Kotlin; and 38 CVEs resolved in Apache Camel. By Michael Redlich
infoqArticles.author: Michael Redlich

infoqArticles.title: Pinterest Uses Event Time Watermarks to Finalize Petabyte Scale Data Partitions
infoqArticles.description: Pinterest has introduced event time-based partition finalization for its database ingestion framework. The mechanism uses Apache Flink to track event time and Apache Iceberg metadata to publish a non-regressing watermark, helping downstream jobs determine when continuously ingested CDC data is sufficiently complete for processing. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: JEP 543 Finalizes Structured Concurrency in JDK 28, Ending Seven Preview Rounds
infoqArticles.description: JDK 28 finalizes structured concurrency through JEP 543, with no API changes from JDK 27. Teams on JDK 27 only need to drop --enable-preview and recompile. Code written for JDK 25 or 26 must adapt to the R_X exception type parameter, ExecutionException wrapping, and the abstract timeout() joiner callback. By A N M Bazlur Rahman
infoqArticles.author: A N M Bazlur Rahman

infoqArticles.title: Article: From Microservices to Agents: the Next Evolution of Distributed Systems
infoqArticles.description: The article examines the transition from microservices to agentic AI architecture in distributed systems. Microservices allow for functional decomposition, while agentic systems focus on decision decomposition. This shift introduces new complexities in observability, reliability, and system design, highlighting the need for updated architectural patterns and practices. By Mallika Rao
